gautam-adani-1.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
gautam-adani-1.confidence: Moderate / legal status well documented; underlying allegation never adjudicated
gautam-adani-1.period: Alleged conduct 2020–2024; US charges and SEC complaint 20 Nov 2024; SEC consent 14 May 2026; DOJ dismissal motion 18 May 2026; court order Aug 2026; SEBI orders Sept 2025 and Sept 2026
gautam-adani-1.summary: Gautam Adani is the subject of three separate legal tracks that must not be merged. (1) The alleged 2020–2024 Indian power-contract bribery scheme: the SEC alleged that he and Sagar Adani orchestrated promises of hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes and misled US bond investors; in May 2026 both consented to SEC judgments without admitting or denying (USD 6 million and USD 12 million penalties). In the criminal case, a federal judge in August 2026 dismissed with prejudice the three counts charged against Gautam Adani (securities-fraud conspiracy, wire-fraud conspiracy, securities fraud) on the Justice Department’s motion, expressly taking no view of the merits and calling the process irregular; the FCPA and obstruction counts, charged only against other, non-appearing defendants, remained undecided at the last reviewed order. No court has found that bribes were paid. (2) The Hindenburg allegations: SEBI’s September 2025 final order found them not established; its September 2026 order found minimum-public-shareholding and fraud allegations not established against twelve noticees (including Vinod Adani) while the group companies and Gautam Adani settled separately without admission. (3) A separate USD 275 million OFAC sanctions settlement by Adani Enterprises, unrelated to the bribery allegation.
gautam-adani-1.mechanism: Alleged payments to Indian state officials → above-market power-purchase commitments (unadjudicated); separately, documented 2026 US process questions about dismissal

support.text: The SEC alleged that Gautam Adani and Sagar Adani orchestrated a scheme to pay or promise hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes to Indian officials in exchange for commitments to buy energy at above-market rates benefiting Adani Green, and falsely touted anti-bribery compliance in a September 2021 bond offering. Each consented to judgment, subject to court approval, without admitting or denying; penalties USD 6 million (Gautam) and USD 12 million (Sagar). Case 1:24-cv-08080 (EDNY).
support.kind: Regulator allegation and no-admission consent settlement

support.text: Garaufis’s order summarizes the October 2024 indictment: it alleged about USD 265 million in bribes for solar contracts, a financing-fraud scheme and an obstruction scheme. Count One (FCPA conspiracy) was charged only against non-appearing defendants; Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Vneet Jaain were charged in Counts Two to Four (securities-fraud conspiracy, wire-fraud conspiracy, securities fraud). These are charging-document allegations recited by the court, not findings. The order also records that Adani Green is India-based and that the SEC complaints allege bribes to Indian state officials.
support.kind: Court recital of charges (allegation, not finding)
support.access: Full 47-page text extracted and read; the order’s printed date is illegible in the text layer, 10 August 2026 is per the SEC notice and press reports

support.text: The same order records that counsel for Adani presented about 600 pages to DOJ, that Principal Associate Deputy AG R. Trent McCotter says he was the sole decision-maker and worked with defense counsel, and that defense counsel twice told DOJ a USD 10 billion US investment could be part of a resolution. The EDNY US Attorney wrote that this proposal was categorically rejected by his office; McCotter says it played no role; Adani swore he knew of no agreement. The judge called the irregularities concerning but stated that the ruling expresses no opinion on the merits.
support.source: US v. Adani, Memorandum & Order, sections I.D–I.F and Conclusion
support.kind: Court record of process (documented, not adjudicated as an exchange)

support.text: DOJ’s one-paragraph Rule 48(a) motion asked to dismiss the whole indictment with prejudice, citing prosecutorial discretion “not to devote further resources” to charges against individuals; counsel for all defendants consented; signed by McCotter and US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr.
support.access: Full 2-page filing and proposed order text read

support.text: On 8 July 2026 the court noted McCotter’s letter raised, for the first time, the possibility of an unmemorialized agreement tied to the dismissal and ordered Gautam Adani to answer by sworn affidavit whether anything was promised, offered or agreed in connection with the dismissal.

OFAC announced a USD 275 million settlement with Adani Enterprises Limited for 32 apparent Iran-sanctions violations (LPG purchases, about USD 192 million in payments, November 2023–June 2025), found egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. This is a corporate sanctions matter, not evidence for the bribery or political-exchange mechanism; it is excluded from the rubric.
support.source: US Treasury OFAC recent actions, 18 May 2026
support.access: Notice page read; the linked enforcement release PDF was not opened

counter.text: Reuters reports Judge Garaufis dismissed the criminal case on 10 August 2026 at prosecutors’ request, said he was satisfied the USD 10 billion pledge did not factor into the decision, and criticized the process. Adani: “I welcome the U.S. Court’s decision with humility and deep respect for the judicial process.” The Adani Group denies wrongdoing.
counter.kind: Subject response and material case update
counter.access: Syndicated summary read; full Reuters text not available

counter.text: The court granted the motion only in part: Counts Two to Four against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Jaain were dismissed with prejudice; judgment was reserved on Counts One and Five against five non-appearing defendants pending DOJ reasons by 31 August 2026. Footnote 44: no one should take the ruling as agreement with DOJ’s decision or an opinion on the merits. No later filing was found in this review.
counter.source: US v. Adani, Memorandum & Order: disposition
counter.kind: Legal status (not a finding of innocence or guilt)

counter.text: The SEC’s covered-action notice lists SEC v. Gautam Adani and Sagar Adani (24-cv-08080) with a qualifying judgment/order date of 10 August 2026; the May release stated the consents were subject to court approval. The notice does not state the type of judgment, so entry of the consent judgments is inferred, not confirmed.

The Adani Group called the DOJ and SEC allegations against Adani Green directors baseless and denied, noted the charges are unproven and defendants presumed innocent, and said it would pursue all legal remedies.
counter.source: b360 Nepal report of the Adani Group statement
counter.access: Short secondary report read; the original statement was not located

counter.text: SEBI’s final order (Kamlesh C. Varshney, whole-time member) found the Hindenburg-linked allegations about transactions with Milestone Tradelinks and Rehvar Infrastructure not established against Adani Ports, Adani Power, Adani Enterprises, Gautam Adani and others: the entities were not related parties under rules then in force, there was no allegation of siphoning, and the money had come back with interest before the investigation. Proceedings disposed of without direction.

The Supreme Court refused to transfer the Hindenburg-related investigation to an SIT or the CBI, found no regulatory failure attributable to SEBI, said third-party reports could not be conclusive proof of inadequate investigation, and directed SEBI and agencies to probe whether Hindenburg’s and others’ short positions involved any infraction. It did not adjudicate the Adani bribery allegations, which arose later.
counter.source: Vishal Tiwari v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 3 (SEBI-hosted copy)

counter.text: SEBI’s 28 September 2026 final order found the minimum-public-shareholding and PFUTP fraud allegations not established against Noticees 1–12 (including Vinod Adani and offshore investors) and penalised two of them for failing to furnish information. Noticees 13–30, including the four listed companies and Gautam Adani, had settled under SEBI’s settlement regulations by separate order, so this finding does not decide their case.
counter.access: Full 81-page order read; the separate settlement order was not opened

counter.text: PTI reports Gautam Adani, four group companies and others settled the MPS case for Rs 1.48 crore without admitting or denying; a week earlier five group companies settled a related-party-disclosure adjudication for about Rs 1.5 crore. Settlements are not findings of guilt or innocence.
counter.source: PTI via The New Indian Express
counter.access: Article text read; the underlying settlement orders were not opened

counter.text: Hindenburg’s January 2023 report alleged stock manipulation, offshore shell networks and accounting issues, and disclosed a short position. It alleged market conduct, not bribery of officials; it is context for the SEBI outcomes above, not support for the political-exchange mechanism.
counter.access: First 100,000 characters of the page read; the later part was not read

gautam-adani-1.limitations: Scope: only the alleged Indian power-contract bribery mechanism and the 2026 US dismissal process are scored. Gautam Adani personally was not charged in the FCPA count; the SEC complaint does attribute orchestration to him. The criminal case is not fully closed on the record read (Counts One and Five, other defendants) and no filing after 12 August 2026 was found. A consent judgment’s entry is inferred, not confirmed. No Indian criminal proceeding, CAG report, Parliament answer or the alleged political relationships with Indian governments were reviewed; Sagar Adani, Vinod Adani and Adani companies are separate persons. Neither the dismissal nor the settlements nor the SEBI findings determine the wider political-economy question, and the allegation is not a finding of bribery.

lakshmi-mittal.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
lakshmi-mittal.period: Sidex privatization and Blair letter, July–November 2001; Commons scrutiny February–March 2002; contrast episodes 2005 (Ukraine), 2013 (India), 2023 (Kazakhstan)
lakshmi-mittal.summary: Forbes lists Lakshmi Mittal under India, but his business is global, so each episode has its own jurisdiction. The scored episode is UK/Romania, 2001–2002: Tony Blair signed a letter supporting Mittal’s company LNM in Romania’s Sidex privatization while Mittal was a £125,000 Labour donor. The overlap is documented; the government said the donation was unrelated and the award decision preceded the letter, and the Commons rejected the opposition motion. Later episodes point the other way and are not averaged into the score: a live-broadcast 2005 Ukrainian re-auction (Ukraine), an Odisha steel plant abandoned in 2013 over delayed iron-ore blocks (India), and the 2023 Kazakhstan transfer of ArcelorMittal Temirtau to the state after a mine disaster (Kazakhstan). No UK/EU case or Indian coal-block case involving Mittal was found in this review.
lakshmi-mittal.mechanism: Party donation and diplomatic endorsement ↔ disputed influence on a privatization (UK/Romania 2001–02)

support.text: Blair told the Commons it was public record that Mittal was a Labour donor, that the letter he signed mentioned LNM rather than Mittal, and that knowing of the support would have made no difference. The Conservative leader’s question confirms the letter to the Romanian prime minister was signed on 23 July 2001.
support.source: Hansard, 13 February 2002 (Prime Minister’s Questions): Blair and Duncan Smith
support.kind: Parliamentary record: acknowledgment of letter and donor status
support.access: Page text of the Commons sitting read on the historic-Hansard mirror

support.text: The opposition motion (moved by Adam Price) noted the £125,000 Labour donation and Mittal’s non-domiciled status and demanded an inquiry; in debate it was argued that the letter followed within days of the request and that Romania sold Sidex in November after an EBRD loan. These are political arguments, not findings.
support.access: Full debate text read on the historic-Hansard mirror

counter.text: Blair said the letter was written at the British embassy’s request to support Romanian reform and, citing the Romanian prime minister, that the award decision was made before the letter; he refused an inquiry.

Wales Secretary Paul Murphy said the donation had nothing to do with the letter, that the letter was sent after the Sidex decision but before signing, and that the EBRD loan reflected its development mandate. Both the motion (192 to 318) and, on the government amendment, the vote (306 to 181) went the government’s way. A Commons vote is not an adjudication.
counter.access: Full debate text and division counts read

counter.text: In a live-broadcast 2005 auction in Ukraine, Mittal Steel won Kryvorizhstal for about USD 4.8 billion after a court annulled an earlier 2004 sale that had been criticized as corrupt; higher bids in 2004 had been rejected. This is the opposite pattern to patronage, in a different jurisdiction.
counter.source: Wikipedia: Kryvorizhstal (secondary compilation of Kyiv Post and others)
counter.access: Page text read; underlying sources not opened

counter.text: In October 2023 Kazakhstan’s president ordered cooperation with ArcelorMittal to cease after a mine explosion killed 46, and ArcelorMittal signed an agreement to transfer ArcelorMittal Temirtau to the state; RFE/RL says Nazarbayev had enticed Mittal to revive the steelworks, but describes increasingly hostile later official treatment. The company said it would compensate victims and cooperate with the state. This shows state power over the company in Kazakhstan, not a finding on earlier relations.
counter.access: Both articles read; Business Recorder at https://www.brecorder.com/news/amp/40270540

counter.text: ArcelorMittal dropped a planned 12-million-tonne steel plant in Odisha, India, saying delays in land acquisition and allocation of captive iron-ore blocks made it unviable. That is evidence against preferential Indian state benefit in that project, not a general finding.

lakshmi-mittal.limitations: Historical single-episode estimate for UK/Romania 2001–02, not a global or present-day assessment, and not a finding that any contract or letter was purchased. Hansard records assertions, not adjudication; the Romanian procurement file and later ministerial inquiries were not reviewed; the earlier receipts from UK Parliament’s own site were replaced by the identical Commons sittings on the historic-Hansard mirror because the original host blocked automated access. The contrast episodes involve other jurisdictions and are secondary or brief. Rampia/Dipside coal-block, EU merger or antitrust matters and Mittal’s UK donations after 2002 were not reviewed.

kumar-birla.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
kumar-birla.confidence: Low / single episode, outcome for Birla personally not fully verified
kumar-birla.period: Allocation 2005; FIR October 2013; CBI closure report August 2014; special-court cognizance March 2015 (secondary); Supreme Court closure of the Singh appeal 29 July 2026
kumar-birla.summary: The Hindalco/Talabira II coal-block episode concerns India. In October 2013 the CBI registered a case alleging that Birla influenced the then coal secretary to get Hindalco added to a block meant for public-sector firms; the Aditya Birla Group denied it. In August 2014 the CBI filed a closure report. A special judge reportedly declined it and took cognizance in March 2015, and the Supreme Court stayed related summons. On 29 July 2026 the Supreme Court, in Manmohan Singh’s appeal, accepted the CBI closure reports and closed the matter on merits. Whether that order separately resolves Birla’s and Hindalco’s own position was not verified. The Supreme Court’s 2014 rulings held coal allocations since 1993 illegal and cancelled 214 blocks as a class, not as a finding against Birla. Birla’s government advisory roles are not scored.
kumar-birla.mechanism: State coal-block allocation → corporate benefit; alleged influence on the secretary, closed by the CBI and not substantiated

support.text: The CBI’s FIR (its 14th in the coal case) alleged criminal conspiracy and corruption: the Talabira II block in Odisha was allocated in 2005 to two public-sector firms, then Birla met the coal secretary, P.C. Parakh, after which the screening committee’s decision was overturned and Hindalco was added. The CBI said it had not quantified the loss. Searches were carried out at group offices.
support.source: The Financial Express: CBI FIR against Birla and Parakh

support.text: The CBI filed a closure report before Special Judge Bharat Parashar in August 2014, having booked Birla as representative of the Aditya Birla Group and Hindalco in October 2013.

A Wikipedia compilation states that on 11 March 2015 a special CBI judge took cognizance against Hindalco, Birla, Parakh and others, and summoned Manmohan Singh; on 1 April 2015 the Supreme Court stayed the summons (the text names Singh and Parakh; one cited headline names Birla, a conflict not resolved here).
support.source: Wikipedia: Indian coal allocation scam (secondary compilation)
support.access: Page text read in part (first 100,000 and part of remaining characters); original reports not opened

support.text: The Supreme Court’s 2014 allocation ruling and cancellation: the Financial Express reported on 25 August 2014 that the Court declared all coal allocations since 1993 illegal, and the CSE release records that on 24 September 2014 it cancelled 214 coal blocks. These concern the allocation process as a class and name Hindalco only as a holder of another block (Mahan).
support.source: Financial Express via India Environment Portal; CSE release
support.access: Both pages read in part; CSE page at https://www.cseindia.org/tag/mining-sector; the judgment itself was not opened

support.text: Bar and Bench reports that on 29 July 2026 a bench led by CJI Surya Kant allowed Manmohan Singh’s appeal against 2015 summons, saying there were no compelling reasons for the trial court to reject the CBI’s closure reports; it accepted the reports and closed the matter on merits. Singh’s counsel had earlier argued the allocation to Hindalco was an administrative decision.
support.kind: Reported Supreme Court order (appeal of a different person)
support.access: Article text read from the page’s structured data (paywalled page); order not opened

counter.text: The Aditya Birla Group denied the charges, saying every process stipulated by the government’s coal-allocation policy was followed and that Hindalco was one of many companies being examined.

The Hindu reports the Supreme Court agreed with two back-to-back CBI closure reports of 2014 giving Manmohan Singh a clean chit and found no sufficient material or good reason to register a corruption case against him; it also faulted the trial judge’s adverse observations. The reading does not by itself decide Birla’s own status.

kumar-birla.limitations: Narrow episode review only. The primary 2014 and 2026 Supreme Court orders, the CBI closure report and the special court’s 2015 order were not opened; 2015 events rely on a secondary compilation. The 2026 order is reported in Singh’s appeal; its effect on Birla and Hindalco is unverified. The earlier Business Today (30 August 2014) receipt from wave 28 could not be re-fetched in this session and was replaced by the 29 August 2014 report. Vodafone Idea government relief measures and other Birla business with the state were not reviewed. Advisory roles are not points by themselves.

savitri-jindal.reviewDepth: Primary-source-led episode review (wave 37); not independently editorially reviewed; not exoneration
savitri-jindal.confidence: Low / family entry, attribution limited, outcomes unverified
savitri-jindal.period: Savitri Jindal: Haryana political office 2005–2014 and 2024; Naveen Jindal/JSPL: coal-block FIRs from 2012 to charges framed July 2019; March 2024 reports of ongoing CBI and ED probes
savitri-jindal.summary: Forbes groups the O.P. Jindal family fortune in one entry, so the individuals must be separated. Savitri Jindal herself holds political office: she won Hisar as an independent in October 2024 and backed the BJP, after quitting Congress and joining the BJP in March 2024. Her son Naveen Jindal (Jindal Steel & Power, MP for Kurukshetra 2004–14 for Congress and re-elected in 2024 for the BJP) is the subject of separate CBI coal-block cases from 2012–2019: charges of conspiracy and cheating were framed in July 2019 over the Urtan North block (alleged misrepresentation to the Screening Committee), and a further Jharkhand block (Amarkonda Murgadangal) case alleged that a former chief minister favoured Jindal firms. The outcome of those cases after 2019 was not verified, no source read alleges misconduct by Savitri Jindal, and Sajjan Jindal (JSW) was not individually reviewed. No score is assigned.
savitri-jindal.mechanism: Public office and family business wealth; for Naveen Jindal/JSPL, alleged misrepresentation to a coal-block allocation body (unresolved in reviewed sources)

support.text: The official Haryana election gazette lists Savitri Jindal as the elected member for 52-Hisar, party affiliation Independent.
support.source: Haryana Government Gazette (Extraordinary), schedule to ECI notification 308/HAR-LA/2024

support.text: All India Radio reported that independent winners including Savitri Jindal extended support to the BJP after meeting Union Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, taking BJP’s tally to 51.

Mint reported that Savitri Jindal, the 84-year-old former Haryana minister in the Hooda-led Congress government, quit Congress and joined the BJP days after her son Naveen Jindal did so; it also stated that Naveen’s company JSPL was being probed by the CBI over irregularities in a Jharkhand coal-block allocation, that the ED was investigating money-laundering charges on the same allocation, and that the ED had searched JSPL premises in April 2022 in a forex case. These are agency-probe reports with agency inputs, not findings.
support.access: Page text read; status after March 2024 not verified

support.text: A Delhi special judge framed charges of criminal conspiracy (IPC 120-B) and cheating (420) against Naveen Jindal, JSPL and four others over the Urtan North coal block jointly allocated to JSPL and Monnet Ispat, the CBI alleging misrepresentation to the Screening Committee about project preparedness.
support.kind: Reported court step (charges framed, not conviction)
support.access: Article text read; later outcome not found

support.text: The CBI filed a final report in a further probe in the Jharkhand Amarkonda Murgadangal case against Naveen Jindal, former MoS Coal Dasari Narayan Rao and others; it alleged ex-Chief Minister Madhu Koda favoured JSPL and Gagan Sponge Iron in the allocation. All accused said there was no evidence of conspiracy and denied the CBI charge sheet.
support.kind: Reported agency allegation and defense response
support.access: Article text read; later outcome not found

counter.text: The reviewed sources allege no misconduct by Savitri Jindal. The Haryana gazette shows elected office only, and Wikipedia’s entry for her lists no controversies; her sons run separate group divisions (Naveen leads JSPL; Sajjan, JSW), so conduct cannot be attributed between them.
counter.source: Haryana gazette; Wikipedia: Savitri Jindal, Sajjan Jindal
counter.access: Gazette read; Wikipedia pages read as secondary compilations at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savitri_Jindal and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajjan_Jindal

counter.text: Both reported coal cases record the accused’s denials; the Hindu article reports only the CBI’s submissions at the charge stage. The Supreme Court’s 2014 cancellation of 214 coal blocks addressed allocations as a class, not the Jindal firms’ conduct.
counter.source: Defense responses in The Indian Express and Hindu; CSE release

counter.text: Wikipedia’s Naveen Jindal page records his Kurukshetra wins in 2004, 2009 and 2024 and joining the BJP on 24 March 2024; it dates the charges to 2019 but names Amarkonda Murgadangal, which differs from the Hindu’s Urtan North, so the Hindu’s wording is used.

savitri-jindal.limitations: Not a score. Forbes’s family entry is not the same as Savitri Jindal’s own conduct; Naveen Jindal’s and JSPL’s cases are corporate and personal to him. Charges framed are not a conviction, and post-2019 outcomes, the 2014 Supreme Court judgment, the CBI FIRs and any ED filings were not opened. No primary court judgments or CBI documents were reached (the Delhi court records host was not available), and the Zee extortion matter, electoral-bond donations and JSW/Sajjan Jindal matters were not reviewed. A review of Sajjan Jindal separately is needed before any family-level estimate. No score follows from office, a surname or family wealth alone.

rationales: The SEC and indictment allege payments to Indian state officials; the allegation is specific but contested and unadjudicated.
Above-market energy-purchase commitments for Adani Green are specifically alleged; no court found them.

The alleged exchange is specific, but no finding, an unadmitted civil settlement and a criminal dismissal on which the judge took no merits view limit inference; the 2026 investment-pledge discussions are documented but disputed and unadjudicated.
The Prime Minister’s signed support letter and Mittal’s donor status are acknowledged on the parliamentary record.
A specific privatization benefit coincided with political support; causal advantage is disputed and the government says the award preceded the letter.
The donation–endorsement–EBRD loan–sale sequence is concrete but a reciprocal bargain is not established; later episodes in other jurisdictions are not averaged in.
